1.pericope_label: Ananias comes down with an orator

schools.summary: Gill counts the five days from the arrival at Caesarea rather than from the seizure in the temple, and notes that the Alexandrian copy reads after some days, leaving the number undetermined. He holds that the priests came down willingly and of their own accord rather than merely as accusers summoned by the chief captain, wishing to vindicate themselves and their people lest they fall under the Roman governor's displeasure for encouraging tumults and riots — the high priest being conscious that he had acted illegally in ordering Paul smitten on the mouth in the midst of the council, and the elders knowing what hand they had had in the conspiracy against his life. Calvin makes the journey itself an argument about the office: it was not meet for the highest priest to take such a journey, so that some other man was highest priest at that time and Ananias, being one of the chief priests and in great authority, took the embassage upon himself. He reads the train of elders as calculated display, that the governor might be moved by their very pomp, and finds the hiring of a rhetorician a sign of an evil conscience, since Paul used no eloquence and needed none answered; eloquence is the gift of God, but here they went about nothing else than to deceive the judge with it, meaning not merely to prove him guilty but to dash him so out of countenance that he could not defend himself.

Henry marks the reversal of roles. Those who had been his judges now appear as his prosecutors, and Ananias, who had sat to judge him, stands to inform against him, disparaging himself and forgetting the dignity of his place — he is not ashamed to own himself a sworn enemy. The elders attended to signify their concurrence and to invigorate the prosecution, since they could find no ordinary solicitor who would follow it with the violence they desired. He supposes that Lysias had told the accusers they must follow Paul to Caesarea if they had anything against him, perhaps expecting they would not take the trouble — but what will not malice do? No time is lost, all other business laid aside to prosecute one man, so intent are evil men to do evil; and the pains they take in an evil matter should shame us out of our coldness and indifference in what is good. Of the advocate he says that the high priest and elders, spiteful as their own hearts were, did not think their own tongues sharp enough, and retained a man probably noted for a satirical wit, giving him a good fee, likely out of the temple treasury which they commanded.

Clarke reckons the five days from the apprehension at Jerusalem and sets out Calmet's scheme day by day, Paul seized as the seven days of his vow were nearly ended, before the council on the sixth, at Caesarea on the seventh, and the priests coming down five days later, the twelfth from his arrival. He opens the chapter with an outline of the whole and takes Tertullus for a Roman proselyte to Judaism, since he speaks everywhere as a Jew, noting that Roman advocates were found in the provinces, spoke both Greek and Latin, and were useful for their knowledge of Roman law and custom. Wesley says only that Ananias would spare no trouble on the occasion, coming with several of the elders, members of the sanhedrim.

Barnes takes the five days as the twelfth day after the arrival at Jerusalem, the interval occupied in receiving the summons and making arrangements, and infers a settled habit of employing Roman lawyers, since the Jews were largely ignorant of Roman customs and of the mode of administering justice. Ellicott thinks the interval just allowed messengers to go from Caesarea to Jerusalem and the priests to engage their advocate, though he allows that dating it from Paul's departure agrees better with the twelve days Paul himself reckons. He places such orators in most provincial towns of the empire, ready to hold a brief for either side, and disposes of the notion that the hearing was in Latin: proceedings before a procurator and his provincials were of necessity in Greek, as with our Lord and Pilate, and Luke, who records when Paul spoke Hebrew and when Greek, would hardly have passed Latin over. Robertson observes that this was a deputation of elders with the high priest rather than the whole Sanhedrin, with no hint of the forty conspirators or the Asian Jews, and thinks the divided council left Ananias and the Sadducees to lead the prosecution; the word for orator means a forensic advocate and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, the name being a diminutive of Tertius, and the verb rendered informed amounts to a formal indictment.

themes: why the priests came in person

schools.summary: Gill settles the smaller question first, that the man called forth was Paul and not the orator, the Latin version putting it beyond doubt by reading that Paul was cited; he was ordered out of custody to hear his indictment and answer for himself. Of the exordium Gill notes that the Jews are made to say they observed the governor's provident care of their nation with pleasure and commended his conduct wherever they came, and that the closing plea covers an omission — the orator could have said a great deal more, but for brevity's sake left it, and because he would not tire the governor's patience or hinder business. Calvin objects not to complimenting a judge at all, which is not always at odds with the lawful form of pleading, but to this compliment, which is altogether corrupt, since the rhetorician insinuates himself under false praises in order to darken the matter in question. To what end speak of peace and a well-ordered state, except that Felix might think the safety of Judaea consisted in condemning Paul and examine the matter no further? Josephus shows how covetously, cruelly and voluptuously the man behaved in that province, the murder of the high priest Jonathas being already past and the emperor soon obliged by the complaints of the whole nation to put another in his place; so we see how shamefully this orator lied, and since all Paul's adversaries sing the same song, we see them blinded with hatred, betraying the state of their own country and caring nothing what befell it so Paul might die.

Clarke divides the speech into exordium, proposition, and narration with conclusion, and grants that the praise had some foundation: bad a governor as Felix was, he had suppressed a formidable banditti under Eliezar, put down the sedition raised by the Egyptian impostor who seduced thirty thousand men, and quelled a grievous disturbance between the Syrians and the Jews of Caesarea. Yet the man is well known from his own historians and from Josephus to have been mercenary, oppressive and cruel, of all which the Jews brought proofs to Nero. He judges the exordium artful enough though lame, and adds that its author had a very bad cause and that few with so bad a one could have made better of it. Wesley grants it nothing: a speech how different from Paul's, which is true, modest, solid and without paint, whereas this has a lame introduction, a lame transition and a lame conclusion — did not God confound the orator's language? Felix, he adds, was a man of the most infamous character and a plague to all the provinces over which he presided.

Barnes allows the compliment a basis in fact, since Felix had arrested a band of robbers under Eleazar and sent them to Rome, had taken the Egyptian false prophet who led four thousand men into the wilderness, and had repressed the sedition between the inhabitants of Caesarea and of Syria; but the words were said in the customary style of flatterers, and stand in contrast with the honest opening of Paul's reply. He glosses the providence as foresight, skill, vigilance and prudence, and cites Wetstein on the claim to accept it always and in all places — what we do in your presence, we do also in your absence. Ellicott finds the administration offered little opening for panegyric beyond the suppression of the sicarii, and admires the emphasis laid on quietness, noting a curious coincidence in Tacitus, who ends his account of the quarrel between Felix and the governor of Galilee with the words that quiet was restored to the province. He renders the next phrase as reforms or improvements, and observes that the Greek word for providence then carried a higher sense than forethought, the tendency to clothe emperors with quasi-divine attributes having put the providence of Caesar on their coins and medals — Tertullus extending the term to a procurator. He catches the tact of the sycophant in the closing plea, where the speaker professes to restrain himself from further panegyric, and marks the contrast between the hired orator's epithet of clemency and the righteousness, temperance and judgment to come of which Paul afterwards spoke to the same ruler. Robertson is blunter, since Tacitus also declares that Felix secretly encouraged the banditti and shared their plunder; but it sounded well to praise him for keeping a peace Tertullus was about to accuse Paul of disturbing. He traces the reform word from its use for setting right broken limbs, and calls the whole a campaign speech which doubtless pleased its hearer.

schools.summary: Gill explains the force of the opening word, which signifies the pest or plague itself, and notes the forensic habit behind it: Roman orators wishing to represent a man as wicked and dangerous to the state called him the pest of the city or of the empire, as may be observed repeatedly in Cicero. On the temple charge he says it rested on nothing but the supposition and conjecture of the Asiatic Jews that a Greek had been introduced, which was false and groundless; and on the complaint against Lysias, that the designs interrupted were not to judge Paul according to law but to kill him after the manner of the zealots. He notes that the chief captain's order was given only after Paul had addressed the people from the stairs, pleaded before the sanhedrim, and been found to be the object of a plot — so that the insinuation of a hindered legal process is false. Calvin wonders at the count about the Nazarenes, since to be a Nazarite was rather a praise than a dispraise among the Jews, and supposes the word to mean not those lawfully consecrated to God but the tumultuary assassins who took to themselves the specious name of zealots, though he allows that others read it simply as Christians. Of the temple charge he says it was light and almost frivolous before a Roman governor who would not have cared if the temple were turned upside down, but nothing was fitter for procuring uproars, and it carried the further implication that a matter of religion belonged properly to Jewish judgment — whence the complaint against Lysias for robbing them of their right, made by way of insinuation because they dared not accuse him openly. Calvin finds the closing request fair on its face but reads the motive: they had their witnesses ready and hoped that fine words would make the governor hand over a man they had already condemned in their own minds.

Clarke counts four particulars in the accusation — that Paul is a pest, that he excites disturbances, that he heads a sect which should not be tolerated, and that he attempted to profane the temple — and matches the first from Martial, thou art not a vicious man, Zoilus, but thou art vice itself. He prefers the reading commotions to sedition, and follows Bishop Pearce in taking the next clause as stirring up tumults against all the Jews rather than among them, since otherwise the orator accuses his own countrymen of rising at Paul's instigation, whereas he wishes to present them as a persecuted people. The word for ringleader he explains as a military phrase for the officer standing on the right of the first rank. The temple charge he calls heavy if it could have been substantiated, since the Romans permitted the Jews to put to death anyone who profaned the temple, and traces it to the calumny about Trophimus the Ephesian; on the claim that they would have judged Paul by their own law he observes that, had Lysias not interfered, they would have murdered him on the spot, and he takes the phrase about great violence to mean rather with an armed force. He judges the whole plan judicious and artful, and says no bad cause was ever more cunningly managed.

Barnes explains that Tertullus did not say Paul was a pestilent fellow but that he was the very pestilence itself, our translation weakening the original; the word rendered sect is the one from which heresy comes but properly means a party, and Nazarene was the name usually given to Christians by way of contempt, while the word for ringleader is properly military, denoting one who stands first in an army. Ellicott takes the world to mean the Roman empire, notes that this is the first appearance of the term of reproach transferred from the Master to the disciples, and observes that the temple charge has been quietly modified, since what was once an assertion that Trophimus had been taken inside is now only an attempt. The advocate throughout identifies himself with his clients, so that the tumult becomes a legal arrest by temple officers which should have been followed by a religious trial; the words from according to our law to come unto thee are absent from many manuscripts, and if genuine are an attempt to make Lysias the real disturber of the peace. On the closing invitation Ellicott suspects a technical term and that the judge was being invited to examine the prisoner by scourging or some other torture, Tertullus keeping back the fact that Paul was a Roman. Robertson observes that moving insurrections was an offence against Roman law if it could be proved, quotes Furneaux's catalogue of what might have been alleged from the plots at Damascus to the riot at Ephesus, and concludes that specious proof could have been produced but was not, the orator passing on to charges with which a Roman court had no concern. He is certain the disputed words are a later addition, missing from the chief uncials and contradicting the earlier narrative, and answers Ellicott on the examination: torture was out of the question for a Roman citizen, and the word means no more than hearing what Paul had to say.

debates.question: What did Tertullus invite the governor to do when he spoke of examining?

simply hear what Paul had to say, torture being out of the question for a Roman citizen

outliers.note: reads the sect of the Nazarenes not as Christians but as the assassins who called themselves zealots, so that the charge quietly enrols Paul among the men the Romans most hated

themes: the pestilence, not a pestilent fellow
what sect of the Nazarenes meant

schools.summary: Gill observes that Paul kept silence under the charge until the governor beckoned with hand or head, since he might not speak for himself until leave was given. Calvin notes that the defence does not argue the quality of the act but denies the crime outright — not that Paul was ashamed of the gospel or afraid of the cross, but that this was no place to make a full confession of faith; so, omitting the cause of the gospel, which his accuser had never touched, he answers simply to the crimes charged. Calvin calls this a sincere and free manner of defending, to set matter against words, and meets the objection that a long governorship could not tell Felix when Paul arrived in Jerusalem: the point is rather that a man long acquainted with the temper of the nation is likely to deal more moderately, since want of skill makes judges too credulous and drives them to make too much haste. He notes also that Paul does not commend the governor's virtues, but says only that he is glad to have to do with a man of experience who may judge the more justly.

Henry sees in the reply a great deal of the spirit of wisdom and holiness, and an accomplishment of Christ's promise that it should be given his followers in that same hour what they should speak. Paul did not interrupt, but let the orator finish, according to the rules of decency and the method of courts, that a plaintiff be allowed to close his evidence before the defendant pleads; and when his turn came he did not fly out into passionate exclamations against the iniquity of the times, nor make any reflection upon Tertullus, whom he knew to be speaking for his fee, but levelled his defence at those who had employed him. Here are no flattering compliments such as the orator used, but something more truly respectful — the profession of a man who answers cheerfully because his own heart does not reproach him, and who does not stand trembling at the bar. He would not say what he could not justly say, that Felix was a judge of inflexible integrity who hated bribes; he said only what was true, that Felix had been many years a judge to this nation, and drew two things from it: that no complaint against Paul had ever come before him in all that time, so that Paul was no such dangerous criminal as they represented; and that he knew the temper of the nation, how bigoted and furious they were against all who did not comply with them, and could therefore make allowance for what came of party malice. Henry adds the positive account of the visit, that Paul came up to worship God in peace and holiness and to keep up his communion with the Jews, not to affront them.

Clarke sets out the plan of the defence — an exordium allowing the judge's competence, then refutation of the three charges and affirmation of three things: that Paul had preserved a good conscience toward God and men, that so far from polluting the temple he had been purified in it, and that his accusers could produce no witness against him. On the years he reckons the sixth or seventh of the administration, which may fairly be called many when the very frequent removals of provincial governors are considered, and he glosses the word judge as answering to the Hebrew term for a ruler or governor, the title of the ancient governors of Israel. Wesley disposes of the compliment in a line: there was no flattery in this, it was a plain fact, for Felix governed Judaea six or seven years and was therefore not unacquainted with Jewish rites and customs, and so the more capable of deciding such a cause. He finds the answer corresponding exactly to the three articles of the charge — against sedition, that Paul had not been long enough in the city to form a party and attempt an insurrection; against heresy, that he confesses himself a Christian but holds the religion perfectly agreeable to the law and the prophets; and against profanation, that he behaved in the temple peaceably and regularly, his innocence having been manifest even before the sanhedrim, where the authors of the tumult did not dare appear against him.

Barnes remarks that Paul did not begin as Tertullus had done, with a flattering address or any art of rhetoric, but founded his plea on the justice of his cause and on the fact that Felix had experience enough of Jewish affairs to judge impartially; knowing the man's character as he did, he would not by flattering words declare what was not strictly true. He explains the many years from the history: Felix and Cumanus had been joint governors, and when Cumanus was condemned the government fell entirely to Felix, some seven years before this — long enough to have learnt the customs of the Jews, and long by comparison with the short tenure of his predecessors. Ellicott sets the apostle's frank manliness against the servile flattery of the advocate, puts the figure at about six years, and defends the phrase on the ground that it exceeded the usual length of a procuratorship; he notes that the verb rendered answer is the one behind our word apology in its older sense of vindication. Robertson agrees that Paul goes as far as he can in the way of a compliment and no further, the governor having merely nodded to him to begin.

debates.question: What does Paul gain by noting the length of the governorship?

positions.position: a judge of that experience can weigh the temper of the nation and allow for party malice, and had never had a complaint against Paul before him
not knowledge of the facts but moderation, since want of skill makes judges credulous and hasty
a competent tribunal — experience enough of Jewish affairs to judge the merits impartially

outliers.note: explains why the gospel itself goes undefended here: a criminal trial was no place for a full confession of faith, and the accuser had never touched the gospel, so Paul answers only the crimes charged

schools.summary: Gill observes that Paul was so far from moving sedition that he never so much as entered into conversation with anyone on any subject, whether civil or religious — not that disputing in the temple was criminal, since it was common for the doctors to dispute in its porches and courts, as they often did with Christ, but he mentions it to show how little he had done; he was indeed found in the temple, but purifying himself according to the law of Moses. On the challenge he notes that the burden lay on the accusers to set the charges in a clear light and give demonstration of them, and that failing this Paul ought in course to be acquitted. Calvin observes that Paul need not have denied any of it had he done it, since he might have answered that it was well done: he had been one of the scribes who disputed daily, neither law nor custom forbade assembling to be taught, synagogues stood in several parts of the city for that purpose, and Christ and his apostles had done the same, so that he might easily have retorted the charge on adversaries who used the very same practice. But since his aim is only to refute the false accusations and to prove that importunate men had molested him for no cause, he treats not of the lawfulness of the fact but of the fact. On the profession of coming to worship Calvin meets a harder question: how can Paul say this when the religion of the temple was already abolished and every distinction of place taken away? He answers that Paul neither lies nor dissembles, since the servants of Christ were not forbidden to worship in the temple provided they did not tie holiness to the place but lifted up pure hands without choosing between places; it was lawful for Paul, being void of superstition, to use the solemn rites there, since he offered no propitiatory sacrifice contrary to the gospel — religion did not compel him to come up as the law had once required, yet he does not abhor an external worship which was to men a testimony of godliness.

Clarke reads the twelve days as the answer to the charge of sedition, the improbability of which is shown from so short a stay, quite insufficient to organise a sedition of any kind; nor could a single proof be furnished that Paul had seduced any man or unhinged him from his allegiance by subtle disputations, whether in the temple, the synagogues or the city. The charge therefore fell to the ground self-confuted, unless they could bring substantial proof, which he challenges them to do.

Barnes gives Beza's reckoning of the twelve days — one spent coming up to Jerusalem, one with James and the apostles, six in fulfilling the vow, the ninth bringing the tumult and the rescue by Lysias, the tenth the council, the eleventh the plot and the removal to Caesarea — the days of confinement there not being counted, since nobody would pretend that a man raised sedition from a prison. The point of the arithmetic is improbability. He notes that the vaguer accusation of being a pest was too general for Paul to trouble with, and that the Greek is not quite what the English suggests: not that worship was the purpose of the journey, but that Paul was engaged in devotion when the tumult arose, his main design being to carry the benefactions of the Gentile churches. Ellicott takes the clause about worship as the implied answer to the profanation charge, since a man who had come to worship was not likely to be guilty of it, and notes that the answer traverses every part of the indictment — not a discussion in the temple, not a crowd gathered anywhere in the city — ending with a demand for adequate evidence, meaning two or three witnesses independent and agreeing. Robertson observes that Paul takes up the very word Tertullus had used for taking knowledge and repeats it back, that the word rendered prove means to set a thing beside its claim, and that the accusers have made assertions and not backed them; Paul, he adds, had no hired lawyer to plead for him but made a masterly plea for his freedom.

outliers.note: insists that Paul could have justified the disputing rather than denying it — Christ and the apostles had done as much — but confines himself to the fact rather than its lawfulness, because refuting the accusation was all that the occasion required

themes: the arithmetic of the twelve days

14.pericope_label: The Way they call a sect

schools.summary: Gill notes that Paul was never ashamed to own what was true, but ready to bear his testimony for it whatever the consequence, and that the hope professed here is of an interest in God and of enjoying eternal life and happiness with him in a future state. Calvin weighs at length what the concession of the name means. He thinks Paul means either that he is a Pharisee, as he had lately confessed, or that he calls the Jewish religion and the gospel that flowed from it a sect without reproach, both standing apart from the usage of every other nation; among Christians the Spirit of God commands that heretics be counted detestable, since heresies bring plague, dissension and wasteness upon the Church, but the Jews openly boasted of their sects and the word carried no infamy before a heathen judge. Paul, though a citizen of Rome, confesses that he continues in the religion he learned of the fathers, and touches his adversaries in doing so, since he worships the same God they worship and in the manner delivered by his ancestors. Calvin adds a caution against misusing the verse: the Papists are ridiculous who make Paul approve all manner of antiquity, for he never meant to ground religion in the authority of ancestors — a defence which would serve every superstition of the Gentiles equally — but only to wipe off the blot of impiety cast on him. On the hope he thinks the order deliberate: having first professed that he believes the Scripture, Paul then adds the hope of a resurrection, so that it may appear the hope comes neither from carnal sense nor from the decrees of men but is conceived out of the word of God. He presses the words about the just and the unjust against those who restrict the rising to the members of Christ, since by the plain voice of Christ all are cited, some to judgment and some to life.

Clarke asks why a neutral word was used to injure Paul and answers from the politics of the council. The term carried no bad meaning among the Jews, the Pharisees themselves being called a sect and Josephus, himself a Pharisee, speaking of the sect of the Pharisees; but two accredited parties already existed with their interests fairly balanced, both represented in the Sanhedrin, and the fear was that the Nazarenes would form a third and divide the influence of both — which is why the Christians had both for enemies, and why the charge of plotting against the state, once laid against Christ, was now laid against his followers as a proper engine for bringing a jealous government into action. On the positive half of the answer Clarke has Paul bringing in no new object of worship and no new creed, acknowledging the Law and the Prophets as divinely inspired and never in the smallest measure detracting from the authority of either; and on the hope, that he holds nothing different from the general belief of the people concerning a future state, since the resurrection of the dead is what they themselves allow. Wesley corrects the appellation on the same ground, not that the word was odious but that it was not honourable enough — a party or sect is formed by men, whereas this way was prescribed by God; the apostle had already said enough for his defence, but takes a fair occasion to make an ingenuous confession of his faith here, his hope in the next verse, and his love a little later. That the resurrection is of both the just and the unjust, Wesley adds, was peculiarly proper to be observed in a public court.

Barnes complains that the English imports our idea of error in doctrine where the Greek says only party, so that the explicit reference of Paul's answer to the prosecutor's word is lost; he notes what Paul does not stoop to answer, the contempt buried in the name Nazarenes, and finds the appeal to the God of his fathers fitted to reach a Jewish hearer, since it showed he had introduced no new object of worship. On the hope he observes that the resurrection was held by the Pharisees present, so that in this cardinal point Paul maintained nothing they did not, and they could not arraign him for it. Ellicott notes that the noun rendered heresy is the same the prosecutor used for sect and should have been translated alike, since as it stands the reader cannot see that the Way had been called a heresy at all; in choosing the term the Way, Paul adopts what the disciples used of themselves and protests by implication against a more invidious epithet. He prefers to render the verb as serve rather than worship, the word being wider in range, and takes the profession of believing all that is written as the denial of the second charge, since Paul's faith in the authoritative standards of Judaism was as firm as any Pharisee's — whether that belief led to the conviction that Jesus was the Christ being a question of interpretation with which Felix had nothing to do, and which Paul, making a formal defence before a Roman ruler, declines to answer. Ellicott sees the same tact as when Paul divided the council earlier, since he identifies himself not merely with the Pharisees but with the bulk of the nation. Robertson finds the confession frank and full: Paul is guilty of that and says so, but prefers his own word, claiming Christianity to be the whole and real Judaism rather than a sect of it, no deviation from it but its fulfilment. He reports the objection that Luke misrepresents an apostle who held to no resurrection save for those in Christ, and rejects it as a mistaken reading.

debates.question: Does the resurrection Paul professes extend to the unjust?

positions.position: yes — the words are pressed against those who restrict the rising to the members of Christ, since all are cited, some to judgment and some to life
yes, and the objection that Luke here misrepresents Paul, who held to no resurrection save for those in Christ, is a mistaken reading of him

outliers.note: explains the sneer in the word sect from the arithmetic of the council: two parties already held the Sanhedrin in balance, and a third would have divided the influence of both, which is why Pharisees and Sadducees alike opposed the Nazarenes

themes: the resurrection of just and unjust

schools.summary: Gill reads the herein as pointing back to the doctrine of the resurrection, which is a doctrine according to godliness that promotes and engages to a holy life, whereas the contrary tends to encourage a dissolute manner of living; the apostle studied and laboured and bent himself to this, employing his thought, care and time upon it. On the errand he reckons a long absence from Jerusalem, some five and twenty years since his conversion, most of them spent among the Gentiles, and notes that the offerings in hand were those of the Nazarites when the Asian Jews found him. Calvin makes the same connection a general rule, that there is no sharper prick to drive men toward a godly and holy life than the hope of the last resurrection, as the Scripture teaches in many places; and he turns it on those who lack it, since an evil conscience is as good as a thousand witnesses to convict men of not believing an eternal life they never long after. He divides the claim in two, an inward sense which regards God alone and the faithfulness toward men that comes out of it, and notes that the word always signifies perseverance in a straight course, so that those truly hope for the resurrection who are never weary of well-doing. Of the errand he says that Paul had not been at Jerusalem for a long time but was conversant in far countries, and came now to bring alms and to offer the sacrifice of thanks — which shows the ill nature and unthankfulness of a nation that recompensed so evil a man who had deserved the goodwill of them all. Calvin adds that this verse expounds the earlier one about worship, since Paul plainly did not travel in order to sacrifice but reports what the Jews found him doing, and that it clears him of both crimes at once: the purifying witnesses that he did not pollute the temple, and the absence of any multitude leaves no ground for a charge of tumult.

Clarke ties the verse back to the creed: because Paul believes there will be a resurrection of both just and unjust, and that every man shall be judged for the deeds done in the body, he exercises himself day and night — toward God in entertaining no opinion contrary to his truth and offering no worship contrary to his dignity, toward men in doing nothing he would not wish done to himself on a change of circumstances, and in withholding nothing by which he might comfort and serve them. On the errand he draws out what it cost: though long absent from his own country, and his political relation to it almost dissolved, Paul came not to disturb the peace of society but brought alms to his nation, the fruit of his own earning and influence among a foreign people, and offerings to God and his temple — proving his attachment to his country and his reverence for its worship. Of the Asian Jews he observes that the very men who stirred up the persecution found him purified in the temple, regularly performing the religious vow into which he had entered, giving no cause for suspicion, with no tumult and no number of people by whom a seditious purpose could have been accomplished. Wesley notes the edge in the sentence with two words, that Paul exercises himself as well as they.

Barnes takes the verb as making conscientiousness the leading habit of a life, and argues that a conscience void of offence requires two things, that it be rightly informed as to duty and that what is known to be right be honestly performed. On the errand he observes that a man who came to bring relief to a suffering people can hardly have come to defile their temple, the alms being the charities of the churches for the poor Christians of Judaea. Ellicott takes the herein to mean in this belief: because Paul held the resurrection as a stern reality, the one law of his life was to keep his conscience clear of wilful sin — words almost as bitter to Felix as to Ananias, though the governor at least had the decency to listen in silence. He sets the interval at four years since the previous visit, which he thinks throws light on the earlier compliment about many years, and notes that this is the only mention in the whole book of the collection which fills so large a place in the letters of the period, an undesigned coincidence between history and epistles often dwelt on by writers on the evidences. He detects a refined courtesy in the word nation, commonly used only of the heathen, where Paul avoids the more usual people and the assumption of superiority it would have carried before a Roman magistrate. Robertson notes that the same verb gives us the word ascetic, and that Paul claims to be at least the equal of his accusers in taking pains to please God; on the adjective he is more precise, since the papyri use it to mean free from hurt or harm and it can be read either actively, as not stumbling, or passively, as not stumbled against — the first fitting the clause about God and the second that about men. He adds Furneaux's remark that it must have been wormwood to Ananias to hear Paul repeat the very words for which he had once ordered him struck on the mouth. He reads the phrase as at an interval of several years rather than after many, and takes the offerings to be the sacrifices mentioned earlier for the four men and himself.

debates.question: How long had Paul been away from Jerusalem?

positions.position: four years, since the previous visit — which bears on what many years meant in the compliment to Felix
an interval of several years rather than many, if the earlier visit is the one meant
some five and twenty years since his conversion, most of them spent among the Gentiles

outliers.note: finds both senses of the adjective at work in one phrase — not stumbling, toward God, and not stumbled against, toward men — so that the clause divides exactly as Paul divides it

themes: the resurrection as a rule of life

19.pericope_label: The witnesses who did not come

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Asian Jews were the only persons who had seen Paul in the temple and knew what he was doing, and that they raised the mob by a hideous outcry, so that all the rest took the matter on hearsay from them; the men now present are the high priest and the elders who came down to accuse. On the one voice he holds that Paul does not concede it to have been an evil in him, only that it was the one thing any of them — and a part of them only, the Sadducees — could judge evil. Calvin observes that the sentence is imperfect but the sense plain: these men of Asia had caused a tumult without cause, and Paul complains of their absence, as if to say that those who lay so much to his charge cannot tell how the matter stands but bring before the governor's seat a tale rashly believed, while the men who set all on fire do not appear. Having retorted the crime upon others, Paul takes courage and appeals to the adversaries who are present, willing them to utter freely anything they know against him. Calvin takes the appeal as made to the council rather than to the governor's bench, and draws the inference from their silence at the time: they knew nothing then to lay to his charge, since they began to stir only at that one word about the resurrection of the dead, from which it appears that they now coin a new accusation for no cause — had there been any real fault in him, they would not have concealed it then.

Clarke sharpens the contrast: the Jews of Asia were the most competent witnesses, declared enemies though they were, and the men who had stirred up the persecution — why then are they kept back? Because they could prove nothing; let those who are here depose, if they found any evil in him when he was examined before their council at Jerusalem. On the one voice he spells out the arithmetic: the Sadducees who belong to that council and deny the resurrection may indeed blame him for professing his faith in it, but the doctrine is credited by the nation in general, there is nothing criminal in such a belief, and nothing else can be brought against him — so that this is the sum of all the charges he is called to answer. Wesley draws the wider moral, that the world never commits greater blunders, even against its own laws, than when it is persecuting the children of God, and grants of the one word only that it was nevertheless the real truth.

Barnes puts the consequence plainly: the only competent witnesses to what happened in the temple had stayed away, which showed they were not prepared to face examination, and the charge ought therefore to be dismissed. He calls the appeal to those present a bold one, showing full consciousness of innocence, and grants their competence for the one occasion they had witnessed. He reports the construction put on the closing words by Chubb and other infidels, that Paul is confessing he was wrong to have cried out before the council, his conscience reproaching him for time-serving and for setting the two parties at odds on purpose; and he answers that Paul is doing nothing of the kind but fixing attention on the main thing he had said, which really was the chief doctrine he had been defending. Ellicott supposes the originators of the disturbance shrank from the consequences of what they had begun and either stayed at Jerusalem or set out homeward when the feast was over; he prefers the reading of the better manuscripts, what wrong act they found in me, and marks how narrow the ground has become, since this was the single instance in which any words of Paul's had even been the occasion of an uproar, and what he then said was a belief he held with their best teachers. Robertson points out that the words about certain Jews from Asia have no verb, a thoroughly Pauline anacoluthon, and quotes Furneaux to the point: the accusers who were present had not witnessed the alleged offence, and those who could have given first-hand evidence were not present, so that there was no case in a Roman court. He notes that the word for wrongdoing is chosen from the accusers' point of view, and adds Furneaux's remark that to a less sensitive conscience Paul's conduct before the council would have seemed venial enough.

debates.question: Is Paul conceding that his cry before the council was a fault?

positions.position: no — he is fixing attention on the main doctrine he had been defending and daring them to prove it wrong; the charge of time-serving is an infidel gloss
no — it is the one thing any of them could call evil, and only a part of them, the Sadducees, at that

outliers.note: turns the silence of the council into evidence: they stirred only at the word about the resurrection, so a real offence would not have been kept back then, and the present accusation is newly coined

themes: no case in a Roman court
the one voice about the resurrection

schools.summary: Chrysostom reads the delay as management rather than caution. Much close investigation was made by many over a long course of time, so that it could not be said the trial was hurried over; but because the orator had mentioned Lysias, Felix deferred them — putting them off on purpose, not because he wanted to learn, but as wishing to be rid of the Jews. On their account he did not like to let the prisoner go, and to punish him was not possible, since that would have been too barefaced. That he gave Paul liberty and forbade none of his acquaintance to minister to him shows that he too entirely acquitted him of the charges; yet to gratify them he detained him, and, expecting to receive money, called for him the oftener.
Gill notes only that Felix had heard what was said on both sides, by plaintiff and defendant alike, the charges and the answer to them, as a judge ought to do.

Henry supposes Felix had a more perfect knowledge of that way than the high priest and elders imagined, having picked up at Caesarea, where Cornelius the centurion was, the notion that Christianity was not the evil thing it was represented to be, and knowing some of that way to be honest men and very conscientious. He reads the excuse as a plain one — when the chief captain comes down I shall know the truth, whether this Paul did go about to raise sedition; you are parties and he is an indifferent person, and either Paul deserves punishment for raising the tumult or you do for raising it yourselves and charging it upon him. Henry then weighs the outcome both ways. It disappointed the priests that Paul was neither condemned nor remitted to their judgment, which he takes for an instance of God restraining the wrath of his people's enemies by the agency of strangers rather than friends, since even a man who knows something of their way cannot but appear for their protection. But it was an injury to Paul that he was not released, for a judge who saw plainly that nothing but malice lay behind the prosecution ought to have avenged him of his adversaries and delivered him out of the hand of the wicked; it is a wrong not only to deny justice but to delay it, and this judge neither feared God nor regarded man.

Clarke finds considerable difficulty in the verse, the manuscripts and the translators differing, and prefers the renderings of Wakefield and Calmet, which both put the inquiry in the future — when Lysias the captain has come down, and after I have gained a more exact knowledge of this doctrine, I will inquire fully into your business. He thinks this the more likely because, before Lysias ever came down, Felix sent for Paul concerning the faith of Christ, evidently that he might be the better qualified to judge when the business came again before him. Wesley takes the clause the same way and adds that Felix, being afterwards better informed, doubtless transmitted a full account of these things to Rome, as Festus and Agrippa did after him.

Barnes lays out the two readings: one takes it that although Felix knew the doctrine better than Paul's accusers did, he nevertheless deferred the hearing until Lysias should come down; the other, which Barnes prefers with Beza, Grotius, Rosenmuller and Doddridge, makes the knowledge a thing still to be got — after I have been more accurately informed of this way, when Lysias has come down, I will hear the cause. He thinks the second confirmed by what follows, since Felix afterwards sent for Paul and heard him concerning the faith, evidently to inform himself; and he notes that Lysias had been acquainted with the excitement and its causes and could be regarded as an important witness. Ellicott observes that the comparative implies a reference to an average standard, that Felix was too well-informed to be moved by the declamation of Tertullus, and that he could see the prisoner was no common assassin. Such knowledge might have been picked up at Jerusalem, which a procurator would visit at the great festivals, or at Caesarea itself, where Philip the Evangelist had founded a community five and twenty years before that numbered Cornelius and other Roman soldiers; and Drusilla, being a Jewess, may have contributed something. He finds the sequel worse than the adjournment, since it turned into an indefinite postponement — perhaps the accusers, having fired their last shot, judged the case lost and withdrew — and observes that detaining a prisoner so was a common incident of Roman provincial justice. Robertson leaves the comparative open in another direction: Felix knew more accurately than the council supposed, though how he came by the knowledge is nowhere stated, and he adds the possibility that Felix knew of the ruling given at Corinth by Gallio, which treated Christianity as a form of Judaism. He says the governor knew perfectly well that the prosecution had failed; the pretext of needing Lysias in person was plausible and false, since Lysias had already declared Paul innocent in writing and was never summoned to Caesarea.

debates.question: Does the verse say Felix already knew the Way, or that he meant to find out?

positions.position: that he meant to find out — after I have been more accurately informed, when Lysias has come down, I will hear the cause
that he already knew it, better than the council supposed, and deferred the case notwithstanding

outliers.note: takes the show of thoroughness as the point of the delay — the long investigation ensured nobody could say the trial was hurried, while the real motive was to be rid of the accusers without either releasing or punishing the accused

themes: where Felix learnt of the Way
an adjournment that became a postponement

schools.summary: Gill states the bare position, that Paul was neither condemned nor acquitted and so had to be kept in custody, watched and guarded that he should not go away, until one or other was done. Calvin argues from the leniency that Felix, though he pronounced nothing on the matter, perceived Paul to be burdened with no fault of his own but with the malice of the priests; the courteous and remiss usage confirms it, since he put a centurion in trust with him that he might have the more liberty. From the permission itself Calvin draws another inference, that Paul's companions and the rest of the church had not forsaken him, since there would have been no point in granting his friends and acquaintance access unless they were present, showed themselves careful for him, and were desirous to do their duty by him; and from their example we should learn that, so long as we may and are able, we must not defraud the martyrs of Christ of any manner of comfort while they labour for the gospel. Of the wife Calvin allows that she had not quite abandoned the feeling of religion she had from a child, since Felix would neither have desired to hear Paul nor vouchsafed to speak with him but for her sake; yet such revolts, he judges, are tickled with curiosity rather than moved by a sincere desire to learn. He recounts her history — daughter to the elder Agrippa, betrothed to Epiphanis son of Antiochus, who would not take on him the rites the Jews used as he had promised, then given by her brother to Azizus king of the Emesenes, and enticed away by the flattery of Felix, who was taken with her singular beauty and employed one Simon, a Jew born in Cyprus, to allure her — so that this voluptuous woman broke faith with her former husband and married an uncircumcised man contrary to the law.

Clarke takes the liberty granted to mean that Felix freed Paul from the chains by which he was bound to the soldiers who kept him, and reads the phrase about his own people as covering his fellow apostles and the Christians generally, free to furnish him with the conveniences and comforts of life and to visit as often as they pleased. This was ample proof that Felix found no evil in him, and he would certainly have dismissed him but for two reasons: he wanted to please the Jews, who could depose grievous things against his administration, and he hoped to get money from the apostle or his friends as the purchase of his liberty. Of Drusilla he notes that Felix was thrice married and that two of his wives bore that name, one a Roman, the niece or granddaughter of Antony and Cleopatra mentioned by Tacitus, the other this Jewess, daughter of Herod Agrippa the Great, affianced at six years old to Epiphanes of Comagene, whose refusal to embrace Judaism led her brother to refuse to ratify the marriage; married about the year fifty-three to Azizus, who received her on condition of being circumcised, and taken from him by Felix through a pretended Jewish magician of Cyprus. She was on the whole a person of indifferent character, though one of the finest women of that age, and is said to have perished with a son she had by Felix in an eruption of Vesuvius. Wesley says the confinement was gentle and Paul only a prisoner at large, by which the gospel was spread more and more, not to the satisfaction of the Jews, though they could not hinder it; and he gives the same account of Drusilla, persuaded to forsake Azizus and marry a heathen, and consumed afterwards with her son at Vesuvius.

Barnes takes Felix to have been disposed to show Paul every favour consistent with safe keeping, esteeming him a persecuted man and the charges malicious, and suspects the access allowed to friends was calculated, so that the prisoner might be furnished with means to purchase his freedom. He traces Drusilla's history from Josephus: daughter of the elder Herod Agrippa, betrothed to Epiphanes on condition that he embrace the Jewish religion and released when he refused, then given by her brother to Azizus king of Emesa, who consented to be circumcised; Felix saw her, fell in love, and sent Simon, a Cyprian Jew who passed for a magician, to persuade her away, and she was prevailed on to transgress the laws of her forefathers. She was therefore living in adultery with him, which Barnes thinks the reason Paul afterwards pressed the subject of chastity. Ellicott would render the officer as the centurion, either the one to whose charge Lysias had committed him or the one who had the care of prisoners awaiting trial, and finds the leniency a measure of the impression Paul had made: the clemency on which the orator had complimented Felix was not dead, but it was shown to the accused instead of the accusers. Of Drusilla he notes that she can scarcely have been ignorant of the new society, since she must have known of the death of James and the imprisonment of Peter, and may have connected her father's end in this very city with the part he had taken against the faith; her presence at these interviews suggests that she was eager to learn more of the faith in Christ, and the procurator and his wife were apparently in the first stage of an earnest inquiry which might have led to a conversion. Robertson glosses the word for indulgence as the opposite of strict confinement, though the man was still under guard, and notes that of these intimates we know the names of Luke, Aristarchus, Trophimus and Philip. He sets the family record out starkly — her father murdered James, her great-uncle killed John the Baptist, her great-grandfather the children of Bethlehem — and suspects the phrase his own wife marks the occasion as no formal trial, Page holding that her curiosity procured the interview.

debates.question: What brought Felix and Drusilla to send for Paul?

positions.position: an earnest inquiry in its first stage, which might have led to conversion
curiosity in the wife, which such revolts feel rather than any sincere desire to learn
the governor's wish to have the prisoner feel his dependence and buy his liberty

outliers.note: reads the permission given to Paul's friends as evidence about the church rather than the governor — the liberty would have been pointless had the brethren not been present and pressing to serve him

schools.summary: Gill notes that the apostle did not confine himself to the doctrine of faith in Christ but insisted on the duties of religion, and reads the first head not as justifying righteousness, which belongs rather to the doctrine of faith, but as the exercise of justice and the doing of right between man and man — agreeable to the light of nature, to the law of God and to the gospel, a virtue highly necessary in a judge and greatly wanting in this one, whom the historian charges with much cruelty and injustice throughout his government. Calvin marks the reversal of positions. Felix had hoped to take pleasure in the sermon, as men desirous of novelty feed their ears with subtle disputations, and to satisfy his wife's desire without trouble to himself; instead he is made to feel a force of the word of God he never thought of, which drives away all his delights. Paul out of bonds disputes of the judgment of God, and the man who had power to put him to death or save his life quakes as before his own judge, finding no comfort but to send the speaker away. Calvin sees in this what force of the Spirit of God there was in Paul's heart and tongue, since, having to speak in the name of Christ, he does not behave like an underling but declares his embassage with a grace as from on high, forgetting that he is in bonds; and he takes it for a fulfilment of the promise that the word of God was not bound with him. He then makes the general rule: the reprobate may be struck with the judgment of God and yet not be renewed to repentance by terror alone, since Felix, touched at hearing that God will judge the world, flees the judgment seat he fears — a feigned sorrow that does not work salvation. True repentance requires a fear that breeds a hatred of sin and presents a man before God willing to be judged by his word, and the token of real profiting is that a sinner seeks his medicine where he took his wound.

Clarke defines the three heads as the principles and requisitions of justice between God and man and between man and his fellows, chastity or self-government with regard to the appetites and passions, and the day of retribution in which the unjust and the incontinent must account for the deeds done in the body; and he matches each to a vice, since Felix was tyrannous and oppressive in his government, lived under the power of avarice and unbridled appetite, and had shown his incontinence in depriving the king of Emesa of his wife, while Drusilla, who had forsaken the husband of her youth and forgotten the covenant of her God, deserved the strongest reprehension under the same heads. He reports Bishop Pearce's explanation of the trembling, that Felix feared lest Drusilla, being a Jewess who knew she had acted against the law of Moses, should be influenced by the discourse and his happiness with her disturbed; and he answers it, since her first husband had been dead about three years and she is said to have turned heathen for the sake of Felix — so we may hope Felix felt real regret for the iniquities of his life, his conscience not being so seared as to keep out every gracious impression. On the dismissal he supposes the man's conscience had received as much terror as it could bear, and that he wished by privacy to hide the confusion evident by then in his countenance. Wesley calls this the only effectual way of preaching Christ to an unjust and lewd judge, and laments the sequel: how happily might the conviction have ended had he pursued the views then opening on his mind, but like thousands he deferred them to a season that never came, and though he heard Paul again he was terrified no more. Drusilla, being used to hear of a future judgment and trusting perhaps to her descent from Abraham or to the expiations of the law, was proof against convictions that seized her heathen husband — which should teach us to guard against every dependence that would reconcile the hope of salvation with an unholy life.

Barnes cautions that the word rendered reasoned means simply discoursing and proves nothing about the form of the address, though the topics make an argumentative discourse likely. He takes the first head as justice in the relations of life rather than the justice of God particularly — a fit opening, since dispensing justice was the man's office, and a judge who took bribes needed reminding of a Being who cannot be bribed. The second means not abstinence from drink but restraint of all the passions, and what Paul had in view was the adultery in which Felix was living. Barnes observes that his boldness is the more striking because he was dependent on this judge for his pardon: a timeserver would have flattered the man's vanity or palliated his vices, but the idea never seems to have occurred to Paul, whose aim was to defend the truth and, if possible, to save the souls of both his hearers. Of the trembling he notes that the Greek does not say the body was agitated, only that the man was alarmed and terrified, and calls it a remarkable instance of the power of conscience that under the preaching of a prisoner the judge should be thrown into such alarm. Ellicott adds a definition from the ethical writers, that the second word describes a man who controls the passions ministering to sensuality while still falling short of a perfect harmony between reason and emotion, and presses the choice of topics: it would have been easy to bring the pair over had the preacher been content to speak smooth things and put the patch of a ceremonial Judaism on the old garment of a sensual life; instead he pressed home what their state needed, and there is as yet no mention of the forgiveness of sins or of fellowship with Christ, which would have been premature. Conscience, he says, was not dead but silenced by a will that would not listen, and Felix treats Paul as Antipas had treated the Baptist, becoming the type of the millions whose spiritual life is ruined by procrastination. Robertson says Paul turned the tables round, expounding the faith in Christ as it applied to his hearers: righteousness they did not possess, self-control they did not exhibit, a judgment certain to overtake them. He notes that the conviction seems to have reached the governor only, since like another Herodias Drusilla's resentment was rather to be feared, and reads the promise of a convenient season as an excuse for dodging the personal turn the sermon had taken.

positions.position: at his own past sins and the apprehension of a judgment to come, conscience acting under truth he was unused to hearing
for his domestic peace, lest Drusilla be moved by the discourse — Bishop Pearce's view, which Clarke reports and rejects

outliers.note: makes Felix the type of a whole class rather than a single failure, since the postponement to a convenient season, and not the resistance itself, is what ruins millions

schools.summary: Gill explains where the expectation came from: Felix had observed from the defence that Paul came up to Jerusalem to bring alms and offerings, and perceived from the indictment that he stood at the head of a large body of men and was a person of consequence, in great esteem among some sort of people, whose life and liberty were valuable. Even if Paul had no money of his own, his friends might furnish enough to obtain his freedom; and it may be, Gill suggests, that this was why the governor ordered that they should have free access to him and minister to him, that so he might have something to give. Calvin observes that Felix, having thoroughly tried Paul's integrity, was ashamed to take money from the Jews for condemning him, and yet, being a covetous man given to corruption, would not acquit him for nothing — which is why he calls for him often, that he may with fair words put him in some hope of deliverance, judges that gape after money insinuating themselves in just this way when they mean to make room for a bribe. Whence we gather, Calvin adds, that the fear which took Felix when he heard Paul dispute was vain and transitory, since hope of gain now compels him to call for the man whom fear compelled him to send away. As for how he could hope for reward from a poor man and one destitute of help, Calvin answers that such judges are sagacious in these matters: seeing the Jews sue so earnestly to have Paul put to death, Felix scented that this was none of the common sort but a man in great favour with many, and did not doubt that many of his friends would willingly bestow cost to redeem him.

Clarke meets Bishop Pearce's question, how Luke could have known the governor's private motive, by pointing to Paul himself, with whom Felix held frequent conferences and to whom he undoubtedly expressed the wish. He calls it the most unprincipled avarice united to injustice: Paul had proved his innocence, his accusers had retired in confusion when the defence was finished, and had Felix been influenced by the common principles of justice the prisoner would have been discharged at once; instead he was detained on the hope of a ransom, since he was evidently a respectable character with opulent friends and at the head of a numerous sect to whom he was deservedly dear. Clarke adds a judgment on the man's origin, that Felix had been a freedman of the Emperor Claudius and consequently once a slave, and that the stream rises not above its source — the meanness of the slave still apparent, and made insufferable by the authority and influence of a governor. Low-bred men, he concludes, should never be entrusted with the administration of public affairs. Wesley calls it an evil hope, and no marvel that a man whose eye was not single profited nothing by all Paul's discourses; the money was to come from the Christians for the liberty of so able a minister, and waiting for it, unhappy Felix fell short of the treasure of the gospel.

Barnes points out that Paul had proved his innocence and should have been released at once, but that Felix, influenced by avarice, kept him in custody hoping that a man wearied with confinement would seek his release by a bribe. Paul offered none: he knew what justice was, and would neither purchase what was his due nor gratify a man who prostituted a high office for gain. The Roman governors in the provinces were commonly rapacious and avaricious like this one, taking office for its pecuniary advantage and making the procuring of money their leading object. Barnes finds the repeated interviews the strangest feature of all, since it might seem remarkable that the man did not fear being alarmed again; but the hope of money overcame it, and when sinners have once resisted the strivings of the Spirit they often sit unconcerned under the very truth that once alarmed them. Ellicott renders the participle as hoping also, continuing the previous verse and so placing the greed in more immediate connection with the procurator's conduct; this greed of gain in the very act of administering justice was the root-evil of a weak and wicked character. He had caught at the word alms, and reasoned that Paul was not without resources, having money himself or wealthy friends. Ellicott finds it easy to imagine what passed in the interviews — the suggestive hints, half promise and half threat, the steadfast refusal of the prisoner to purchase a freedom he claimed as a right, and his fruitless attempts to bring about a change for the better in his judge's character. Robertson notes that Roman law demanded exile and confiscation for a magistrate who accepted bribes, but that it was lax in the provinces and Felix had doubtless received them before, Josephus representing him as greedy for money; he catches the persistence in the tenses, since Felix kept on hoping, kept on sending and kept on communing, and was doomed to disappointment — he was never terrified again.

debates.question: How could Luke know what Felix privately hoped for?

positions.position: from Paul himself, with whom Felix held frequent conferences and to whom he undoubtedly expressed the wish

outliers.note: uses the renewed summons to date the earlier trembling: a fear that gives way to the hope of gain was vain and transitory, since the same man sends for the preacher whom terror had made him dismiss

themes: where the expectation of money came from
the interviews and what passed in them

schools.summary: Gill is careful about the reckoning: the two years are not of Felix's government, since he had been judge in that nation many years, but of the apostle's confinement at Caesarea. Calvin observes that departing governors commonly released such prisoners as they knew to be innocent, and that Felix took the contrary course to win favour. The Jews had often complained of his filthy gain, his extortion, cruelty and unruly government, and the emperor, wearied with so many complaints, called him out of Judaea; so that, to keep them from spiting him too sorely, he leaves Paul bound, making the guiltless servant of God a kind of offering for his own evil deeds in order to appease the priests. Calvin infers something about Paul from the same fact: knowing that a judge who gaped for gain would have turned favourable the moment money was offered, and having time enough to gather it, Paul plainly not only spared the brethren the cost but detested a bribery by which the holiness of civil order is shamefully polluted.

Clarke dates the two years from Paul's coming as a prisoner to Caesarea, and puts Festus into the government of Judaea about the year sixty, the sixth or seventh of Nero. Felix, having failed to get the money he expected, hoped to prevent complaints against his administration by leaving Paul in some measure in the hands of the Jews, it being customary for governors on leaving a province to do some public beneficent act in order to make themselves popular. But he gained nothing by it, since the Jews pursued him with their complaints even to the throne of the emperor: Josephus relates that when Festus was sent as successor the principal Jewish inhabitants of Caesarea went up to Rome to accuse Felix, who would certainly have been brought to punishment had not Nero yielded to the importunate solicitations of his brother Pallas. Thus, like the dog in the fable, by snatching at the shadow he lost the substance; he hoped for money from the apostle and got none, and sought the friendship of the Jews and miscarried. Honesty, Clarke concludes, is the best policy, and he that fears God need fear nothing else. Wesley says the same in a line, that men of the world stretch forth their hands to the things of God to gratify one another, and that the wisdom of Felix did not profit him or satisfy the Jews at all, their accusations following him to Rome and having utterly ruined him but for his brother's interest with Nero.

Barnes notes that Paul was unjustly detained the whole time, and that the object in leaving him bound was to conciliate the Jews and prevent their accusing the outgoing governor before the emperor for the evils of his administration. He quotes the historian's own sentence — that when Festus was sent as successor, the principal inhabitants of Caesarea went up to Rome to accuse Felix, who would certainly have been punished had not Nero yielded to the solicitations of Pallas — and calls the agreement with Luke an undesigned coincidence, since Josephus never mentions Paul, yet establishes that Felix had every reason to court Jewish favour just then. The plan failed twice over, Barnes adds: he sought money by injustice and failed, and sought the favour of the Jews by injustice and failed in that also, so that the inference from the whole transaction is that honesty is the best policy. Ellicott points out that the Greek inverts the English, reading that when a period of two years was accomplished Felix received Porcius Festus as his successor, and is cautious about filling the silence: some have assigned the letter to the Hebrews to these years and others the letters to Ephesus, Colossae and Philemon, but there is no adequate evidence for either, and it is better to think of the apostle's patient resignation and of his intercourse with Philip and the church at Caesarea. He suspects that Luke, who had come with him to Jerusalem and sailed with him from Caesarea, was not far off during the imprisonment, and that the evangelist used the opportunity to collect materials for his two histories. Ellicott adds that the change of administration was caused by the complaints of the Jews, that the influence of Pallas saved Felix from further punishment, and that Festus, who came to the province about the year sixty, is described by Josephus as suppressing the robbers who infested the country. Both he and Robertson render the phrase about showing the Jews a pleasure as a banking figure, to deposit a favour, Ellicott calling it an investment in iniquity whose boon was not meant to go without return. Robertson explains the recall from the open fight between Jews and Gentiles in the market-place at Caesarea, which Felix put down with the soldiers at the cost of many Jewish lives; he notes that Paul lingered in prison waiting for a second hearing that never came, thinks it probable the material of the third Gospel was gathered and part of it written in this period, dismisses the attempts to place the imprisonment letters here as more specious than convincing, and reports the reading of one manuscript that Felix left Paul bound on Drusilla's account, she disliking him as much as Herodias disliked the Baptist.

debates.question: What was written, if anything, during these two years?

positions.position: probably the material of the third Gospel was gathered and part or all of it written, the imprisonment letters belonging elsewhere
nothing can be assigned with adequate evidence; better to think of the apostle's patient resignation and Luke's gathering of materials

outliers.note: turns the failed bribe into evidence of Paul's own conduct: with time enough to raise the money and a judge who would have taken it, he neither burdened the brethren with the cost nor stooped to a bribery that pollutes the holiness of civil order

themes: a favour deposited with the Jews
